note: Two chains only. Doing this across the map is the collaboration being proposed, not the thing being given away. Both expectations were committed before any link analysis existed (commit bbfa54f); links and findings were added afterwards, so the ordering is checkable in git rather than asserted.

paths.title: From science case to first light: what sets the elapsed time of a frontier telescope
paths.axis: Elapsed time from first concept study to first light
paths.axes_excluded: Cost per unit of collecting area, and cost per unit of science return. Their gap statement bundles cost with schedule — 'cost-prohibitive and slow' — and the two run over a partly different set of links. Each is a separate chain, and a chain that mixes them produces a binding link that is an artifact of the mixing rather than a property of the world.
paths.expectation: Design and optimisation search helps at the concept and optics stages, and the binding links will fall on the physical build and on the funding decision, neither of which any current AI capability touches. If that holds, the demonstration is that closing every cognitive link in the chain changes the total duration very little. A second prediction, stated separately so it can fail separately: Convergent's three capabilities attached to this gap — modular assembly with reduced launch costs, leveraging commercial component advances, and a space telescope factory — all act on the fabrication and assembly links, and none acts on decision, approval or funding. Both predictions are recorded before any programme history was assembled, and both are testable against published JWST, Rubin and ELT milestone dates.
paths.finding:
Both predictions hold, and the second holds exactly.

Prediction 2 first, because it is the cleaner test. Convergent's three capabilities for this gap are modular assembly with reduced launch costs, a space telescope factory, and leveraging commercial component advances. All three act on links 5 to 7 — fabrication, integration, launch. None acts on links 2 or 3. The prediction was recorded before their capability descriptions were read for this purpose and it is confirmed without qualification. Stated as an observation about the capability set and not as a deficiency: those capabilities are aimed at two of the four binding links, which is a better hit rate than a random three would achieve, and the JWST integration link is the single longest in the chain.

Prediction 1 holds with a refinement worth more than the prediction. Four links bind — strategic ranking, funding authorisation, fabrication, and integration and test — and no current AI capability touches any of them. But which pair dominates depends on the programme, and that was not predicted. JWST is build-dominated: seventeen of its thirty-two years fall after construction started in 2004. Rubin is decision-dominated: thirteen years from the 2001 National Academies recommendation to the August 2014 construction award, against ten years and ten months of construction to first light. The ELT sits between them, with two and a half years of the delay attributable to nothing but a funding condition on an already-approved design.

On the headline claim, the honest arithmetic has two versions and both are given. The generous version treats the entire seven-year science case period as compressible cognitive work: closing every cognitive link then removes about nine and a half of JWST's thirty-two years, under a third, and leaves all four binding links untouched. The realistic version notes that those seven years were consumed by community consensus rather than by analysis, in which case the compressible cognitive links are design maturation and commissioning, about two and a half years, under a tenth. Either way the conclusion is the same and it is the one predicted: closing every cognitive link in this chain leaves a frontier telescope taking more than twenty years.

links.blocker: Community consensus on what to build, not analysis capacity. The step ends when a field agrees on one instrument, and agreement is produced by workshops and committee reports.
links.evidence: JWST: NGST workshop at STScI September 1989; an STScI committee recommends a larger infrared telescope in 1995-1996. Seven years. ESO: OWL concept pursued from 1998, OWL Blue Book published end of 2005. Seven years.
links.rationale: Not binding, and the reason matters for the whole chain. Synthesis and trade-study tools are mature and could compress the analytical content of these seven years substantially. They cannot compress the part that actually consumes them, which is a community converging. Treating the full seven years as AI-addressable is the most generous accounting available and is used below as an upper bound.

links.link: Strategic ranking (decadal survey or council priority)
links.blocker: A fixed external cadence. A project that misses a decadal survey waits for the next one, and the wait is ten years regardless of how ready the project is.
links.evidence: Rubin: planning from the early 1990s, recommended by a National Academies report in 2001, top-ranked large ground-based project only in the 2010 decadal survey, NSF construction award August 2014. Thirteen years from first national recommendation to construction start. ELT: ESO Council names ELTs its highest strategic priority in December 2004; construction green light December 2014. Ten years.
links.rationale: Binding, and binding in an unusual way: the delay is quantised. No amount of readiness moves a project forward inside a decadal cycle, so the marginal value of accelerating everything upstream of this link is zero until a whole cycle is saved. No AI capability in the taxonomy acts on it.

links.blocker: Appropriation, and conditions attached to it. A design can be complete, reviewed and approved and still wait on money.
links.evidence: ELT: ESO Council approved construction in June 2012 on the condition that contracts above 2 million euros could be awarded only once the total cost of 1,083 million euros (2012 prices) was 90% funded; the green light followed in December 2014. Roughly two and a half years of pure funding latency with the design frozen. Rubin: Final Design Review December 2013, National Science Board conditional approval May 2014, construction award August 2014.
links.rationale: Binding, and the ELT case is the cleanest instance available anywhere in this analysis: the delay is explicitly and only about money, with every technical question already settled. Nothing in the capability taxonomy touches it.

links.blocker: Technology readiness for long-lead items, and the design-review sequence.
links.evidence: JWST: TRW/Ball design selected 2002, construction of long-lead components begins 2004, instrument critical design reviews 2006, mission critical design review 2010.
links.rationale: Not binding. This is the link where design and optimisation search is most obviously useful and most obviously mature, which is exactly why it does not set the pace. Two years from contractor selection to construction start is the shortest interval in the chain.

links.blocker: Long-lead optics, cryogenic qualification, and single-source suppliers.
links.evidence: JWST: construction of long-lead components begins 2004; all 18 primary mirror segments complete and cryogenically tested in 2011. Seven years.
links.rationale: Binding. All three of Convergent's capabilities attached to this gap act here or at the next link.

links.blocker: Strictly serial single-string assembly on hardware that cannot be duplicated, so nothing can be parallelised and every anomaly stops the line.
links.evidence: JWST: mirror segments mounted into the backplane 2015-2016, optical and spacecraft elements mated 2019, final environmental testing complete 2020. Nine years from mirror completion.
links.rationale: Binding, and the single longest link in the JWST chain. This is the link a space telescope factory is aimed at, and it is the one where the capability set is most clearly pointed at the right place.

links.evidence: JWST: final environmental testing complete 2020, launch 25 December 2021. Roughly one year. Ariane 5 selected as launch vehicle in 2005.
links.rationale: Not binding. Reduced launch cost, which two of their three capabilities depend on, acts on the cost axis rather than on this one.

links.blocker: On-orbit alignment and calibration of a segmented optic.
links.evidence: JWST: launch 25 December 2021, first full-colour images and start of science operations 12 July 2022. Six and a half months.
links.rationale: Not binding, and the shortest link in the chain by an order of magnitude. Wavefront sensing on eighteen segments is the most technically demanding cognitive task in the whole sequence and it took under seven months, which is the chain in miniature.

paths.title: From draft to credited contribution: what sets the cost of publishing research
paths.axis: Cost, measured as reviewer and editor labour per published paper
paths.axes_excluded: Speed, meaning elapsed time from submission to publication, and inclusiveness, meaning who can afford to publish and who can read the result. Their sentence bundles all three — 'expensive publishing practices restrict and slow the spread of knowledge' and 'more inclusive and dynamic'. Speed in particular behaves differently by venue: journal latency is reviewer-supply-driven, conference latency is set by a fixed programme committee calendar, so a chain mixing them would produce a binding link that is an artifact of the venue mix.
paths.expectation: This chain must produce a different answer from chain 1 or the pair demonstrates nothing. AI does act on several links here: drafting and screening work now, and reviewer-to-proposal matching is tractable, though there is published evidence that traditional statistical representations outperform generative AI at identifying expert reviewers. So the expectation is not that AI does nothing. It is that AI acts on the links that were never rate-limiting, while reviewer recruitment, judgment consistency and the credit and legitimacy step remain untouched. Stated explicitly so it cannot be read the other way: this is not a claim that publishing is a cognitive bottleneck. It is not, and asserting it would be wrong. Recorded before the link analysis.
paths.finding:
Confirmed, and it differs from chain 1 in the way the pair needs it to.

AI is not absent from this chain. It acts fully on links 1 and 2 and on half of link 3, which is more than it touches anywhere in chain 1. The finding is that those are the links that were never rate-limiting. Three links bind — reviewer recruitment, review judgment, and credit and legitimacy — and the first and third are labour-supply and institutional-recognition problems that no matching or drafting system addresses.

Link 1 is the sharpest result and it was not predicted in this form. Drafting is the link where AI has most obviously arrived, and cheapening it made the chain worse rather than better: submissions rose 42% over five years in the one corpus where a journal has published full-submission figures, and the cost moved downstream onto the recruitment link that was already binding. Relieving a non-binding link upstream of a binding one adds load to the binding link. That is standard critical-path behaviour and it is worth stating plainly, because 'AI can help with writing papers' reads as progress on this gap and is closer to the opposite.

Link 3 is where the chain earns the axis choice. Splitting recruitment into matching and willingness separates the half that is a well-posed prediction problem from the half that is a labour-supply problem, and the binding half is the one AI does not touch. The published evidence goes further than needed for the argument: on reviewer identification specifically, traditional statistical representations outperform generative AI.

One observation about their capability set, and it runs the other way from chain 1. Two of the four capabilities they attach to this gap — a post-publication peer review layer, and new protocols for knowledge production and verification — act directly on link 7, the credit and legitimacy link, which is binding. For the telescope gap none of the three capabilities acts on a decision link; here half of them do.

Stated once more because it would be easy to misread: this chain does not show that publishing is a cognitive bottleneck. It shows the reverse. The cognitive links are the cheap ones.

links.blocker: Author time. Historically the most expensive step for the author and the cheapest for the system.
links.evidence: An Organization Science editorial with five-year full-submission-corpus access reports submissions up 42%.
links.rationale: Not binding, and its cost has already collapsed. The consequence is the important part: cheapening this link did not reduce the cost of the chain, it moved cost downstream onto reviewer recruitment. This is the clearest case in either chain of relieving a non-binding link and making the system worse.

links.evidence: ESO reports that classical triage 'has significantly degraded the quality of feedback for the triaged proposals' — screening under load trades feedback quality for throughput.
links.rationale: Not binding on the cost axis. Screening is genuinely tractable for current models, which is why it is already being done and why it does not set the cost.

links.blocker: Willingness to serve, not the ability to identify who should serve. These are different problems and only one of them is a matching problem.
links.evidence: Roughly five invitations per accepted review (Silverchair, Future of Peer Review 2026). A survey of 139 journal editors with 27 interviews finds 55% rate finding reviewers a significant or very significant challenge, and some 'described having to send out 30 or more invitations to secure just two reviewers' (Jamali, Luca and Wakeling, 15 February 2026). Meyerson documents 21 years of declining reviewer acceptance, 2002-2024. ESO, introducing distributed peer review, states that 'it has become progressively harder to find scientists willing to serve in the panels and in the OPC'. And on the part AI could do: traditional statistical representations outperform generative AI at identifying expert peer reviewers, tested on NASA/ADS records and observatory DPR data across 379 researchers.
links.rationale: Binding, and it is the link that most rewards being split in two. Matching is a well-posed prediction problem where AI is applicable and, on current evidence, not even the best method. Willingness is a labour-supply problem that no matching system addresses. The binding half is the half AI does not touch, which is the whole finding of this chain in one link.

links.blocker: Irreducible subjectivity in ranking work that is above the bar.
links.evidence: NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment: two independent committees disagree on 23% of papers, and approximately half the accepted list would change on a random rerun — consistent with 26% in 2014. Cortes and Lawrence, revisiting the 2014 experiment, find no correlation between review scores and later citation impact for accepted papers, and a correlation for rejected ones: 'the reviewing process for the 2014 conference was good for identifying poor papers, but poor for identifying good papers.'
links.rationale: Binding, and unusually well quantified for an institutional link. The Cortes and Lawrence result also sets the bar any automated reviewer has to clear, and it is a low bar in one direction and an unreachable one in the other: filtering bad work is where review already works, ranking good work is where it does not, and it is not established that the second is a solvable problem for anyone.

links.blocker: Editor labour, and accountability for the decision.
links.evidence: Follows directly from the recruitment and judgment links; editors carry the residual cost when reviews do not arrive.
links.rationale: Not binding on the cost axis. Its cost is largely inherited from link 3.

links.blocker: Article processing charges and platform cost.
links.evidence: Three of Convergent's four capabilities for this gap act here or upstream of it: disrupting traditional publishing models, frugal science initiatives, and micro/nanopublishing protocols.
links.rationale: Not binding on the labour-cost axis, and this deserves care because it is the link their gap sentence centres on. On the inclusiveness axis — explicitly excluded from this chain — it may well be binding. That is why the axes were separated.

links.blocker: Hiring, tenure and funding committees decide what counts. Nothing in the pipeline can make them count something new.
links.evidence: A model can review a paper today; it cannot make a hiring committee count that review. The same asymmetry explains why reviewer supply falls: the labour is unpriced and uncredited, and pricing it is an institutional act.
links.rationale: Binding, and the only link in either chain where the blocker is purely a matter of what institutions agree to recognise. Two of Convergent's four capabilities for this gap — a post-publication peer review layer, and new protocols for knowledge production and verification — act here.
